defaults.permitted_development: A change of use in England depends on the lawful existing use, the proposed use class and any specific permitted development route, not on a general householder right. Many proposals still need planning permission, prior approval or both, especially where external works, servicing or intensified activity are involved. In visitor-heavy coastal areas, parking pressure, seasonal use and disturbance to nearby homes often attract closer scrutiny.

rules.height_rules: There is no automatic height allowance for change of use. Any extra storey, plant, flue, lift overrun or roof equipment is separate operational development and must be assessed in its own right.
rules.depth_rules: There is no fixed depth allowance. Rear additions, storage yards, outdoor seating, service areas and enlarged floorspace are separate planning issues from the use change itself.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary effects often decide the outcome: noise, servicing, odour, overlooking, waste storage, deliveries, parking and customer activity can all matter more than the internal use label. In visitor-heavy coastal areas, parking pressure, seasonal use and disturbance to nearby homes often attract closer scrutiny.
rules.roof_rules: New vents, extract systems, plant screens, condensers or roof terraces are not automatically covered just because the use changes. They need their own planning assessment and can be decisive for neighbours.
rules.materials_rules: External alterations such as shopfront changes, shutters, signage, cladding or new openings are assessed separately and should fit both the host building and the wider street scene.
